---
title: "Checking the analysis"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

A step test gives 6 to 12 lactate samples, each with an analyzer error of a few percent, and every threshold is read
off a curve fitted to them. Before trusting a number, ask three questions:

1. **Is the test sound?** A missing resting sample, a lactate dip, a last stage that was not completed.
2. **Does the curve follow the stages?** Regression diagnostics, adapted to so few points.
3. **How sure is each threshold?** How much it moves without one stage, and its confidence interval.

## Is the test sound?

`lactate_checks()` lists what is easy to miss in a table of numbers. The printed results say how many checks need
attention.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)

plateau <- tibble(
  intensity = c(0, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400),
  lactate = c(1.0, 1.1, 1.3, 2.0, 3.4, 5.2, 6.4, 6.4)
)
plateau_results <- lactate_threshold(plateau, intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)
plateau_results
lactate_checks(plateau_results)
```

Here lactate did not rise in the last stage. If that stage was not completed, leave it out:

```{r}
lactate_threshold(plateau, intensity, lactate, method = "Dmax", plot = FALSE, max_intensity = 350)
```

## Does the curve follow the stages?

`lactate_diagnostics()` checks the fitted curve the way a regression model is checked, with the adjustments that 6
to 10 points need, and prints a summary. Here is a trained female cyclist from `lactate_tests`:

```{r}
female <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "cycling_female") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)
diagnostics <- lactate_diagnostics(female)
diagnostics
```

```{r, fig.height = 11, fig.width = 9}
autoplot(diagnostics)
```

Each panel answers one question, and its subtitle says what to look for.

**Fit to the stages.** The curve with the measured stages, and a dashed line from each stage to the curve (the
residual). Look for runs of stages on the same side of the curve, not for single stages a little off it: with an
analyzer error of 2 to 4% ([Bonaventura et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4306774/)), a residual of 0.1 to 0.2 mmol/L is expected.

**Residuals vs fitted.** The residuals against the fitted lactate. They should scatter around zero with no pattern.
An arch (positive at both ends and negative in the middle, or the reverse) means the shape of the curve is wrong for
this test: an exponential, for example, cannot follow stages that stay flat or dip at the start. A fan that widens
to the right is expected, because analyzer error grows with lactate ([Bonaventura et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4306774/)).

**Normality of residuals.** The standardized residuals (each residual divided by its standard error) against the
values a normal distribution would give. They should follow the line. With 6 to 10 points, no test can tell much:
in a simulation of cubic fits to 6, 8 and 10 stages, a Shapiro-Wilk test rejected normality in under 2% of runs,
even when the errors were heavy-tailed or skewed (code below). A check that "passes" means "could not tell", not
"fine". Look for one point far from the others instead.

**Influential stages.** How much each stage pulls the curve, as Cook's distance: how far all the fitted values would
move if that stage were left out ([Cook, 1977](https://doi.org/10.2307/1268249)). Two things are special with so few stages:

* The first and last stages always have a high *leverage* (the potential to pull the curve), by design: leverage
  depends only on where the stages are along the intensity axis, and the ends have no neighbors on one side. For a
  cubic on 10 stages, the end stages here have a leverage of 0.82 and the inner ones 0.24 to 0.33. Because the
  curve bends towards a high-leverage stage, its residual looks small exactly when it matters most, which is why
  Cook's distance combines the residual with the leverage.
* The usual cut-offs fail. The rule "leverage above 2p/n" (p, the number of curve terms; [Hoaglin & Welsch, 1978](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1978.10479237))
  gives 2 x 4 / 8 = 1 for a cubic on 8 stages, a value leverage can never exceed, so it flags nothing. lactater
  flags a stage when its Cook's distance is above the median of the F(p, n - p) distribution, which adapts to n and
  p ([Cook, 1977](https://doi.org/10.2307/1268249)).

**Leave one stage out.** Every threshold computed again without each stage in turn (a jackknife; [Efron, 1982](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611970319)). A
grid has one row per method and one column per stage left out, shaded by how far the threshold moves, with the move
written where it is 3% of the threshold or more, about the day-to-day variation of a threshold ([Heuberger et al.,
2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846)). A pale row means the threshold does not rest on any single
stage; a dark cell names the stage it rests on; a dark column is a stage that many thresholds rest on, which is worth
a second look at its sample. Dropping the first or last stage changes where the D<sub>max</sub> line starts or ends,
so dark cells there are expected for the D<sub>max</sub> family. The jackknife standard error,
`sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((theta_i - mean(theta_i))^2))`, summarizes the spread for each method:

```{r}
diagnostics$jackknife |>
  arrange(desc(jackknife_se)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

**Which curve predicts best.** Each stage predicted by the curve fitted without it. The printed summary gives the
prediction error of the best curve: the root-mean-square difference, in mmol/L, between each measured stage and its
prediction from the curve fitted without it. More on this below.

### When one stage drives the curve

In this trained cyclist, lactate falls after the first stage, probably after a hard warm-up:

```{r}
dip <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "cycling_early_dip") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)
dip_diagnostics <- lactate_diagnostics(dip)
dip_diagnostics
```

The first stage has a Cook's distance of 4.9, five times the cut-off: it pulls the fitted curve. Without it,
Log-log moves by 34 W, while OBLA 2.0, read off the curve higher up, barely moves:

```{r}
dip_diagnostics$leave_one_out |>
  filter(method %in% c("Log-log", "OBLA 2.0"), stage == 120)
```

That does not make the stage wrong: the dip is real physiology, and deleting a measurement to get a nicer curve is
not a check. It means that the first-rise thresholds of this test should be read with care, and that the next test
needs a lighter warm-up. The summary also names LTP1 as the most sensitive threshold, for another reason: with 8
stages, each of the three straight segments of LTP holds only a few stages, and leaving out the 320 W stage moves
LTP1 by 69 W:

```{r}
dip_diagnostics$leave_one_out |>
  filter(method == "LTP1")
```

## Which curve?

`lactate_fit_quality()` fits every curve to the same points. A curve with more parameters always follows the points
more closely, so the RMSE (the typical distance between the curve and the stages) always favors it. The prediction
error does not: each stage is predicted by the curve fitted without it (leave-one-out cross-validation), which
punishes a curve that bends to follow single points.

The elite rider in `lactate_tests` shows the difference:

```{r}
elite <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "cycling_elite") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)

lactate_fit_quality(elite) |>
  select(fit, parameters, rmse, prediction_error)
```

The B-spline follows the stages most closely (the lowest RMSE), but predicts a left-out stage worse than the 3rd
degree polynomial: it follows the noise as well as the curve. The runner is the opposite case: the polynomial cannot
follow the flat first stages, and the spline and 4th degree polynomial predict better.

```{r}
runner <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "running") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, sport = "running", plot = FALSE)

lactate_fit_quality(runner) |>
  select(fit, parameters, rmse, prediction_error)
```

Choose the curve before you look at the thresholds, use the prediction error as a guide rather than a rule, and keep
the same curve between tests of the same athlete. Some methods fix their curve anyway: Exp-D<sub>max</sub> and Log-Exp-ModD<sub>max</sub>
use the exponential, LTratio and IAT the B-spline, and Log-log and LTP the measured stages.

## How sure is a threshold?

The jackknife shows how much a threshold rests on single stages. `ci = TRUE` asks a different question: how much
does it move with the scatter of this test? Every replicate keeps the fitted curve, adds residuals resampled with
replacement (leverage-adjusted and centered; [Davison & Hinkley, 1997](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511802843)), and runs every method again. The interval is
the middle 95% of the replicate thresholds. The overview plot draws it as a line on each row.

```{r, fig.height = 8}
set.seed(1)
with_ci <- demo_data |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE, ci = TRUE, n_boot = 300)

with_ci |>
  select(method, intensity, intensity_low, intensity_high)
autoplot(with_ci)
```

Thresholds read off the fitted curve at a fixed concentration (OBLA) move little. Breakpoint methods (Log-log, LTP)
move a lot, because a breakpoint between two stages can jump to the neighboring interval. The intervals do not
include errors that are the same in every sample, such as analyzer bias or the sampling site, and this bootstrap has
not been validated specifically for lactate thresholds; read the intervals as a lower bound of the uncertainty.

## The simulation of normality tests

<details>
<summary>The code behind the "under 2%" above (4,000 runs per cell; takes a few seconds)</summary>

```{r, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
rejected <- function(n, errors, runs = 4000) {
  x <- seq_len(n)
  truth <- 1 + 0.05 * exp(0.6 * x)
  mean(replicate(runs, {
    y <- truth + 0.3 * errors(n)
    stats::shapiro.test(stats::rstandard(stats::lm(y ~ poly(x, 3))))$p.value < 0.05
  }))
}
error_types <- list(normal = rnorm, heavy_tailed = function(n) rt(n, 3), skewed = function(n) rexp(n) - 1)
tidyr::expand_grid(errors = names(error_types), stages = c(6, 8, 10)) |>
  mutate(rejected = purrr::map2_dbl(errors, stages, \(e, n) rejected(n, error_types[[e]]))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = errors, values_from = rejected)
```

</details>
